verses.note: The land promise defines the space in which Abram's descendants are to live as God's people. Its borders are repeated to Moses and Joshua (Deuteronomy 1:7, Joshua 1:4), and Israel's history returns to it again and again.
From this point ‘Israel’ is both a man and, soon, a people (verse 32). The nation's identity is rooted in this night: a people named for wrestling with God and surviving by his blessing.
The nation carries its ancestor's wound in its daily life. A meal becomes a small act of memory that Israel's identity began with a man who was blessed and lamed by God on the same night.

Ephraim and Manasseh, sons of an Egyptian mother, will be adopted by Jacob as his own (48:5) and become tribes of Israel. Ephraim grows into the leading tribe of the north, so much that the prophets use its name for the northern kingdom (Hosea 11:8). The people of God included Egyptian descent from the start.

The social distance Egypt keeps from the Hebrews helps preserve Jacob's family as a distinct people. Separation that looks like contempt becomes part of how God keeps the family intact until it becomes a nation.
The name Israel marks Jacob as the bearer of the promise at the moment he decides to take the family to Egypt. The descent that begins here will end with a nation brought out in the exodus.
"The sons of Israel" here means twelve brothers; by Exodus 1:7 it means a people. The phrase itself carries the story's claim that the nation is this family grown large.
The shift from singular to plural marks the moment the family begins to become the nation promised in 46:3. Exodus 1:7 picks up the same verbs to show that promise fulfilled.

Twelve individuals become the twelve tribes in this verse. Jesus' choice of twelve apostles, who will judge the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28), and the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem named for them (Revelation 21:12) look back to this moment.

Israel begins as a family with names, not as an abstract nation. Every later list of the tribes (Numbers 1, Revelation 7) grows out of this one, and the God who will call himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (3:6) is the God of a particular family before he is the God of a people.

Israel's identity is given in family terms before it is given in legal ones: God's firstborn son. Hosea recalls it (Hosea 11:1), and Matthew applies Hosea's line to Jesus returning from Egypt (Matthew 2:15), presenting him as the true Son who embodies Israel.

The genealogy and the military term together recast Israel's identity. They are not merely an enslaved labor force but ordered families with names and histories, the LORD's hosts, about to march out under his command.
